📌 Proof of Wallet Ownership: Confirming an Address Without Moving Funds

Main Points
⏺ Sometimes you need to prove a wallet belongs to you without sending a transaction
⏺ A wallet can do this by signing a message with the private key
⏺ This post explains why signatures are useful, but still need attention

1️⃣ Core Idea — the wallet signs a text message, and another party verifies that the signature matches the address.
2️⃣ Why It’s Used — it can confirm wallet ownership for login, access, verification, or campaign participation.
3️⃣ Why It’s Convenient — no gas is needed and no assets move, because the message is not a normal transaction.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — scammers can disguise harmful requests as a simple login or signature.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — check the domain, message text, expiration time, and never sign requests you don’t understand.

Final Thoughts

Message signing is a fast way to prove address ownership. But the “Sign” button should not become an automatic habit: first understand what you are confirming.

Spain exempts self-custody wallets from crypto tax reporting

Spain's tax authorities have confirmed that cryptocurrency held in self-custody wallets — where the owner controls the private keys — does not need to be reported under Form 721, the country's disclosure form for foreign-held digital assets. The exemption hinges on one condition: no third party holds the assets on your behalf.

The rule draws a clean line between personal custody and exchange or custodial holdings abroad, which remain reportable. Simple in principle, potentially significant in practice — Spain just gave self-custody a regulatory edge.

📌 How will ESMA supervise crypto firms under MiCA in 2027? 

📣 The European Securities and Markets Authority has set operational resilience, outsourcing and sufficient EU based operations among its main crypto supervisory priorities for 2027 as the bloc moves further into enforcement of the Markets in Crypto Assets Regulation. 

🌐 ESMA said in its 2027 work program published Monday that its work on MiCA will concentrate on coordinating national regulators and developing more consistent supervision of crypto asset service providers across the European Union. The program comes as the regulator moves from writing and implementing MiCA rules toward overseeing how licensed firms comply with them in practice.  Chair Verena Ross described the change during a meeting of the European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs, saying ESMA’s MiCA work had moved “from rulemaking towards supervision and convergence.” 

⭐️ Operational resilience will be one of the main areas under scrutiny as ESMA works with national competent authorities responsible for supervising CASPs. Outsourcing risks, liquidity, reverse solicitation and the classification of crypto assets are among the other areas identified for coordinated work in 2027. Supervisors will pay attention to whether firms maintain sufficient operations within the EU instead of relying heavily on functions or infrastructure based elsewhere.

Ukraine Warns of Possible New Russian Campaign Against Energy Infrastructure ⚠️


Ukraine has presented European partners with documents that it says contain intercepted Russian plans for attacks on the country’s energy system during the coming winter.

According to Ukrainian officials, the material describes a potential campaign aimed at critical infrastructure serving major Ukrainian cities. The facilities identified in the documents include parts of the electricity network as well as systems connected to heating and water supplies.

The information has emerged as Kyiv and its European allies prepare for another winter in which energy infrastructure is expected to remain a major security concern. Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian power facilities during the war, while Ukraine has sought to strengthen air defenses, repair damaged infrastructure and secure alternative sources of electricity.

The documents presented by Kyiv have not been independently authenticated in public. Their contents therefore represent Ukrainian assessments of Russian planning rather than independently established evidence of what Moscow will ultimately do.

Still, Ukrainian officials regard the material as significant because of the potential scale of the infrastructure involved. Damage to major power facilities can have consequences beyond the immediate loss of electricity. In large cities, interruptions to power can affect district heating systems, water distribution, communications and other essential services.

The timing is also important. Ukraine enters the colder months with an energy system that has already sustained extensive damage from repeated Russian attacks. Engineers and utility companies have spent much of the year repairing substations, generating facilities and transmission networks while attempting to create additional capacity and emergency reserves.

The country has also worked with European governments to reduce the impact of possible disruptions. Electricity imports, backup generation and additional air-defense equipment are among the measures being considered or expanded as Ukraine prepares for another period of heavy demand.

The latest warning comes against a broader backdrop of continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Moscow has previously said that its strikes are directed at military and energy-related targets, while Ukrainian officials have repeatedly accused Russia of deliberately attacking infrastructure essential to civilian life.

The distinction between military objectives and civilian consequences is particularly important in the energy sector. A strike on a power facility can affect hospitals, transportation, water systems and residential buildings even when the facility itself is described as a military or strategic target.

European governments therefore face the task of assessing the credibility of the Ukrainian intelligence while preparing for scenarios that could place additional pressure on Ukraine's power system. 

The documents may provide indications of Russian planning, but they do not by themselves establish whether every element of the reported plan will be carried out.

For Ukraine, the immediate challenge is practical: maintaining electricity, heating and water supplies while protecting infrastructure that is difficult to replace quickly. For its European partners, the issue also involves determining how much additional assistance can be provided before the winter demand period begins.

The coming months will show whether the reported plans translate into a broader campaign against Ukraine's energy network. For now, Ukrainian officials are treating the documents as a warning and are urging partners to prepare for further attacks on critical infrastructure.

📣 Japan arrests two suspect over 81M yen crypto police scam 

🔖 Japanese police have arrested two people suspected of helping a fake police fraud group steal cryptocurrency worth approximately 81 million yen from a woman in her 40s. The victim was allegedly told that her bank card had been connected to a large money laundering investigation. According to police information cited by FNN, the group claimed a fraud case had caused 600 billion yen in losses and that around 400 accounts had been used to launder funds.

⚠️ FNN reported that the caller told the woman her card appeared among accounts connected with the supposed money laundering investigation. The caller then claimed she was close to being arrested and needed to “prove her innocence.” Police allege that the false accusation eventually led the victim to transfer cryptocurrency worth around 81 million yen. The assets were valued at approximately $515,000 using the conversion cited in reports on the case.

‼️ Investigators have not publicly identified the cryptocurrencies involved or disclosed the wallet addresses that received the assets. Available reporting therefore does not establish how the cryptocurrency was subsequently moved, converted or withdrawn. The Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department believes Okayama and Minamisawa participated in a larger organization. Known losses from fraud cases involving the two suspects have reached approximately 240 million yen, according to FNN.
